lesson.title: Running Out First: Determining the Limiting Reagent
lesson.summary: When reactants are not mixed in the exact ratio a balanced equation calls for, one of them runs out first. That reactant, the limiting reagent, alone determines the maximum amount of product the reaction can form.
lesson.body:
Every calculation in Stoichiometry so far has assumed you know exactly how much of one reactant you have, with an unlimited or unspecified supply of everything else, an ample supply of H2, for instance. Real reactions are rarely that convenient. When you mix specific, measured amounts of two or more reactants, they are almost never present in exactly the mole ratio the balanced equation calls for. One reactant will always run out first, and once it does, the reaction stops, no matter how much of the other reactant is still sitting there unused.

A kitchen analogy makes this concrete. A recipe calls for 2 eggs per 1 cup of flour. If your kitchen has 6 eggs and only 1 cup of flour, the flour runs out after a single batch, and the extra 4 eggs go unused no matter how badly you want more pancakes. Flour is the limiting ingredient here. The same logic governs chemical reactions: the limiting reagent is the reactant that gets used up first, and it single handedly caps how much product can form. The reactant that is not used up completely is called the excess reagent.

To find the limiting reagent, compare how much of one reactant would actually be needed to consume all of the other, and see whether you have enough. Take ammonia synthesis again: N2(g) + 3 H2(g) -> 2 NH3(g), confirmed balanced with 2 nitrogens and 6 hydrogens on each side. Suppose a reaction vessel contains 4.00 mol N2 and 9.00 mol H2. Check how much H2 would be needed to react with all 4.00 mol of N2: 4.00 mol N2 times, 3 mol H2 divided by 1 mol N2, equals 12.0 mol H2 needed. Only 9.00 mol H2 is actually available, which is not enough, so H2 will run out before all the N2 is used. H2 is the limiting reagent.

It is good practice to confirm this from the other direction. Check how much N2 would be needed to react with all 9.00 mol of H2: 9.00 mol H2 times, 1 mol N2 divided by 3 mol H2, equals 3.00 mol N2 needed. Since 4.00 mol N2 is available, more than the 3.00 mol required, N2 is confirmed to be in excess, with 4.00 minus 3.00, or 1.00 mol N2, left over once the reaction stops. The amount of product must always be calculated from the limiting reagent, never the excess reagent, since the excess reagent's starting amount overstates what the reaction can actually produce. Using H2, the limiting reagent: 9.00 mol H2 times, 2 mol NH3 divided by 3 mol H2, equals 6.00 mol NH3 produced, which is the real, achievable yield of this reaction.
